cards.title: Run decision debates that surface real evidence before committing
cards.summary: Use the Debate Maker method — frame the question, spark rigor with data demands, then drive closure — to make high-stakes decisions people will actually execute.
cards.use_when: Making a high-stakes store decision where you own it — committing to a new product category, changing fulfillment/3PL, re-platforming, or a major pricing/inventory investment — and you need the team to execute it afterward.
steps: Frame the issue: write down the specific decision question, name who owns the call, identify who should be in the debate, and collect the data before convening.

Spark debate by holding two things at once: create safety (share your own view last, invite opposing stands, focus on facts, depersonalize the issue, look past job titles) and demand rigor (ask hard questions, challenge underlying assumptions, chase why until you hit root cause, attack issues not people, debate both sides).
When someone offers an opinion, ask for evidence — a trend or cluster of data points, not a single anecdote — and make that a standing norm for the group.
Ask each person, not just dominant voices; quieter analytical people often know the data best.
Close by reclarifying the process: state whether the decision is being made now, whether it's a team call or yours, and how differing views get resolved.
Make the call yourself or explicitly delegate it; then communicate the decision and the rationale.
Afterward, summarize key ideas and tell people what will happen with their input so discretionary effort isn't wasted on the next round.
caveats: The source's own finding: Debate Makers are not necessarily consensus leaders — they are equally comfortable making the final call or deferring when it's clearly someone else's domain.
Rigor doesn't mean the loudest voice wins; without the safety half of the practice, hard questions read as attacks and shut debate down.
cards.source_name: Multipliers_ How the Best Leaders Make Everyone Smarter.docx

cards.title: Make the debate visible so the whole store team can execute
cards.summary: Holding decision debates openly in front of interested observers prepares people at every level to execute and learn the norms of rigour.
cards.use_when: Framing a cross-functional store decision — e.g., a seasonal assortment or promotion calendar — where many people will need to act on the outcome but only a few are deciding.
steps: Set up a debate that key decision-makers run at the front, with extra seating around the perimeter and an open invitation to anyone interested in the issue.
Let observers watch the reasoning — the questions, the data, the disagreement — not just hear the verdict afterward.
After the decision is reached, communication of the decision and its rationale requires little effort because the audience already has the context and is primed to execute.
Treat these sessions as training: observers learn what is expected when they later sit at the table for a different issue.

Avoid the antipattern described in the book — the two-circle meeting where an inner circle decides and a silent outer ring only takes notes to relay orders later. That format produces people who debate the soundness of decisions instead of executing them.
caveats: This is a leadership account from the source's research, not a measured retail outcome; the payoff is comprehension and readiness to execute, not a claimed performance benchmark.
Transparency is limited by compensation, legal or confidential commercial information — those debates still need a closed format.
cards.source_name: Multipliers_ How the Best Leaders Make Everyone Smarter.docx

cards.title: Run your own three-question debate opener as a leader
cards.summary: A simplified starter process — ask the hard question, ask for the data, ask each person — for leaders who want to shift from answering to questioning.
cards.use_when: Running a recurring store or merchandising meeting (weekly trade review, assortment planning, pricing review) where you tend to supply the answer first.
steps: Ask the one question that gets at the core of the issue and confronts the underlying assumption. Pose it, then stop — hold your own view and ask for theirs.
When an opinion arrives, ask for the data behind it. Push beyond a single anecdote toward a trend or a cluster of data points; normalize coming into debates with the evidence already assembled.
Ask each person for their read, deliberately pulling in the quieter voices; the source notes that softer voices often belong to analytical people closest to the data.
Reframe your own contribution: your job is to ask the question that produces the thinking, not to have the answer.
Start small — practice these three steps in a single standing meeting before applying them to a high-stakes call.
caveats: The source presents this as an easy starting block, not a complete substitute for the full Debate Maker practice (frame, spark, drive to decision).

The shared-inquiry rule behind it is strict: the discussion leader only asks questions and does not give their interpretation — a rule that can be impractical when you are also the formal decision owner.
cards.source_name: Multipliers_ How the Best Leaders Make Everyone Smarter.docx

cards.title: Give people 51 percent of the vote
cards.summary: Defining a named owner with majority ownership of a domain — and being explicit about your own role — creates confidence and stops second-guessing.
cards.use_when: Assigning accountability for a store function or project: a category, paid acquisition channel, retention/email program or a storefront replatform.
steps: Name the lead and state their stake explicitly in the spirit of "you get 51 percent of the vote and 100 percent of the result."
Clarify your own role at the same time: keep me in the loop, consult me as you go — so they understand the nature of your involvement and when you'll invest.
Signal confidence in the outcome by responding to early updates with expectation of upside rather than auditing the work.

Recognize the behavioral consequence: most people given majority ownership neither second-guess every call to you nor ignore you, but consult on important decisions for a second opinion and act alone on small ones.
Apply it consistently across every function owner so the norm is uniform.
caveats: Attributed to John Chambers' practice as described in the book — a leadership heuristic, not a governance or delegation policy for regulated decisions.
Keep decisions that legally require the owner's sign-off (safety, finance, contracts) out of the delegated 51 percent.
cards.source_name: Multipliers_ How the Best Leaders Make Everyone Smarter.docx

cards.title: Give ownership for the whole result, not the piece
cards.summary: Assigning ownership for a bigger picture rather than a functional slice makes people stretch beyond their scope and integrate with others.
cards.use_when: Setting KPIs or goals for category, marketing, supply-chain and merchandising leads on a store team.
steps: Watch for the failure mode shown by the Big Picture exercise: teams given only a one-inch square optimize that square, then discover their enlarged piece doesn't connect — mismatched lines, unblended colors, a patchwork result.

Instead of measuring each lead solely on their function, give the team a shared measure of the whole outcome — in the source's Intel EPROM example, a division team spanning engineering, manufacturing, marketing and sales each took the same success measure: division profit.
Expect the team then to contribute across functional boundaries because each member's success depends on the whole, not just their slice.
Communicate the shared measure clearly enough that people feel the business is 'ours', which the source says produced heightened engagement.
caveats: The Intel example and the team member's enthusiastic quote are reported case material, not a measured performance uplift.
Shared measures without clear individual role definitions can blur accountability — pair this with named ownership for the domains inside the whole.
cards.source_name: Multipliers_ How the Best Leaders Make Everyone Smarter.docx

cards.title: Stretch the role one level up to grow people fast
cards.summary: Giving people jobs one — occasionally two — levels beyond their demonstrated capability creates a vacuum they grow to fill.
cards.use_when: Deciding who should own a bigger store responsibility — a new channel, a regional market, a complex cross-functional project — when the candidate lacks direct experience.
steps: Assess for smarts and drive rather than exact-match experience; the source's examples include a domestic operations director with no global experience and a marketing manager given a corporate-wide launch.
Assign ownership one level up, occasionally two — not at the level of current capability.
When the person protests their inexperience, acknowledge it and hold the assignment; explicit reassurance that they will figure it out plus your visible backing is what the source describes.
Recognize the experience is often grueling — frame it as such rather than pretending otherwise, and back it with the resources and coaching covered in the Invest Resources practice.
caveats: The source claims Multipliers get roughly twice the capability of Diminishers and 'more than 100 percent' from people — these are the book's characterizations from its research, not measured store outcomes.
Stretching two levels up works in the source's examples; over-reaching without support resources is a risk the source pairs with active investment.
cards.source_name: Multipliers_ How the Best Leaders Make Everyone Smarter.docx

cards.title: Teach through Socratic questions instead of answers
cards.summary: In the moment of a setback, ask questions that surface the team's knowledge instead of supplying the solution yourself.
cards.use_when: Coaching a store team through a real problem — a failed promotion, a stockout, a broken checkout flow — where you can see a fix but want the team to own the learning.
steps: Distinguish teaching from telling: Diminishers tell you what they know; Multipliers help you learn what you need to know.
Insert yourself at teachable moments — when the team is spinning or has just suffered a setback — because minds are most open then.
Ask questions like 'What do we know about what doesn't work?', 'What assumptions led us to these outcomes?' and 'What risks do we face now that need mitigating?'

Even when you know the solution, don't offer it — the source's position is that offering the answer costs you the teaching moment; the approach has to be Socratic, asking the question and teasing out the answer.
Make the short-term cost tolerable: the return is the team's ability to solve and avoid similar problems in future.
caveats: The source's example is an executive at a technical firm wrestling a technical setback; adapting it to ecommerce operations is a reasonable application, not a demonstrated retail result.
Pure Socratic coaching is slow — when an error is already hitting live revenue or customers, the decision to jump in versus teach is a judgment call the source leaves to the leader.
cards.source_name: Multipliers_ How the Best Leaders Make Everyone Smarter.docx

cards.title: Grab the pen, then hand it back
cards.summary: Jump in to teach and unblock, then return the marker and the accountability so the team stays in charge.
cards.use_when: When you step into a struggling workstream — a landing page that isn't converting, a stuck inventory plan, a stalled replatform — and need to help without taking the work over.
steps: Contribute your insight, sketch an emerging structure or line of thinking, and give the team something to test and push against.
Resist the pull to finish the job yourself even when it's late and you can see the ending; the source's cautionary example is the leader who stays at the whiteboard and leaves the team dependent.
Check the owner is comfortable with the new direction before handing control back.
Physically and verbally return ownership — give the pen back and say the team should run with it — because that signals they remain in charge.
Prefer feedback framed as guidance rather than orders; the source's rationale is that someone working on the issue full time for weeks has insight a leader lacks after a few minutes.
Expect the long-run payoff: a team that can act without rescue, which matters because you cannot always be present for the emergency.
caveats: The source's own conclusion: failing to return ownership creates dependent organizations; it is a stated leadership principle from the author's research, not a measured conversion or revenue figure.
There are true emergencies (a breached checkout, a stock-out escalation) where taking over temporarily is warranted; the discipline is in returning control rather than keeping it.
cards.source_name: Multipliers_ How the Best Leaders Make Everyone Smarter.docx

cards.title: Slant your meeting table so accountability rolls back to the owner
cards.summary: Take part in the work without absorbing problems that belong to someone else — keep action items on their side of the table.
cards.use_when: In review meetings where a category owner, channel manager or agent escalates store problems expecting you to take them over.
steps: Engage fully: listen intently, offer carefully dispensed insight, ask great questions, and escalate a critical issue when warranted.
Aim for the end state where problems pushed at you slide back to where they came from by the close of the conversation.

Model restraint on note-taking: the source describes an executive who wrote a single note in a small notebook only when he alone was accountable for an action — and because of that selectivity, those commitments were reliably done by the next day.
Make ownership of the problem, not just the task, stay with the person closest to it.

Give accountability back with two moves: praise the edge of their thinking, then hand back the problem — the source's phrase pattern is 'that's good thinking' followed by 'you're smart, you can figure this out.'
caveats: Attributed to the author's account of leaders he has worked with; the 'slanted table' is a metaphor for a practice, not a measurement.
This is the opposite of the two-in-a-box support practice, which is used when extra brainpower is genuinely needed — choose deliberately between backing off and adding a partner.
cards.source_name: Multipliers_ How the Best Leaders Make Everyone Smarter.docx

cards.title: Add backup without reducing ownership
cards.summary: When a project gets harder, add a second brain as a sounding board while leaving full accountability with the original owner.
cards.use_when: When a store project is knocked off course by a complication — a new company-wide initiative, a supplier change, a platform-wide migration — and the owner is capable but stretched.
steps: Ask whether you would be more disruptive than helpful by jumping in directly; if so, add a peer partner instead.
Set up a two-in-a-box arrangement: the partner joins key planning meetings, acts as a sounding board, and offers support, while the original owner remains fully responsible for the project.
Publicly credit both: praise the owner's leadership and thank the backup for their role.
Signal that the roles can reverse next time — the partner accountable and the original owner backing them up — so backup reads as a development move, not a demotion.
Treat added backup as resource investment that earns the right to hold the owner accountable.
caveats: The source example is a corporate M&A strategy project; applying it to ecommerce operations is a suggested adaptation, not a demonstrated retail result.
Two-in-a-box fails if the partner starts issuing orders — the source is explicit that ownership must not be reduced.
cards.source_name: Multipliers_ How the Best Leaders Make Everyone Smarter.docx

cards.title: Never leave an AWK without a FIX
cards.summary: Require anyone surfacing a problem to bring a proposed solution, building the habit of completing the thinking.
cards.use_when: Managing store team members, agencies or junior staff who report problems rather than proposals.
steps: Make the norm explicit: don't just identify the problem, find a solution. The source's origin story is a leader who returned a marked-up document with 'Don't ever give me an A-W-K without an F-I-X!'
Apply it from the top — it was the author's own edit that got sent back, not just a rule for juniors.
When you receive an issue without a proposal, ask for the fix rather than supplying it.
Frame the request as giving people the opportunity to complete their thinking and exercise intellectual muscles that otherwise atrophy around smart, capable leaders.
Pair it with backup so people aren't stuck: they should know they can bring a draft or consult, just not an open problem.
caveats: The story is the author's internship anecdote, not an ecommerce case study.
Requiring fixes can create noise if the problem genuinely exceeds the reporter's scope — use judgment for issues needing escalation (legal, safety, fraud).
cards.source_name: Multipliers_ How the Best Leaders Make Everyone Smarter.docx

cards.title: Hand over institutional leadership before it becomes a dependency
cards.summary: The founder who insists on turnover — reinvesting in successors and political literacy — so institutions outlive their creator.
cards.use_when: Founder-led store or brand thinking about succession, or a department head building so a function runs without them.
steps: Notice the default: it would have been easy for Elaben to be re-elected to run SEWA indefinitely as its founder.
Instead, invest time educating members about the democratic process so everyone has the political literacy to run for open positions.
Actively turn over responsibility to new and younger leadership rather than assigning tasks from the top.
Invest in the next generation's growth: in the example, every successive chief executive of the SEWA organizations first worked under her tutelage, each given greater ownership as they matured.
Continue investing elsewhere — founding new institutions — while giving guidance only when asked, keeping the influence of a parental figure rather than an operator.
caveats: The SEWA example is a union and cooperative federation with elections and term limits mandated by law; the specifics don't transfer directly to a privately-held ecommerce brand.
The source's motto, 'A leader is someone who helps others lead,' is a principle, not a measured succession outcome.
cards.source_name: Multipliers_ How the Best Leaders Make Everyone Smarter.docx

cards.title: Reclaim the reason-for-doing instead of only assigning tasks
cards.summary: Focusing people on the larger purpose — the 'vast and endless sea' — rather than splitting work and giving orders.
cards.use_when: Onboarding or re-energizing a store team during repetitive, low-visibility work such as order processing, catalog cleanup or inventory counting.
steps: Frame roles around the mission rather than the task list — the saint-exupery line the book opens with asks leaders to teach people to yearn for the sea, not simply gather wood and divide work.

When a Diminisher takes over from a self-owning team, initiative can collapse: the source's caustic example, Marcus Dolan, told a captain never to hold practice without him and lost all ownership; the players stopped initiating entirely.
Notice the signal of best intentions gone wrong — jumping in when stakes are high is tempting; a store version is a manager personally rewriting a buyer's or merchandiser's work instead of coaching.
Return to the mission framing when you catch yourself rescuing: your role is to coach, the team's role is to play.
Accept slower gains in the short term for an organization that can win without your presence on the field.
caveats: The rugby examples are high-school athletics stories illustrating a management idea, not retail performance evidence.
The source's claim that micromanaged teams 'lose every game' is a narrative case, not a benchmark.
cards.source_name: Multipliers_ How the Best Leaders Make Everyone Smarter.docx
